COMPOUND AUTHORIZATION AND CONSENT FOR PARTICIPATION IN A RESEARCH STUDY

 

YALE UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF MEDICINE

CONNECTICUT MENTAL HEALTH CENTER

 

 

Study Title: The COPE Project

Principal Investigator (the person who is responsible for this research): Dr. Al Powers

Phone Number: 203-974-7329

Funding: Burroughs Wellcome Fund

 

Research Study Summary:

  • We are asking you to join a research study.
  • The purpose of this project is to understand perceptual experiences without external stimuli (seeing, hearing, feeling things that others do not) and learn from the methods and skills individuals with these experiences have developed to further enhance mental health treatment for those who struggle. This part of the study aims to compare vision perception as well as belief formation and reward processing in people with and without a history of psychedelic substance use (psilocybin mushrooms, LSD, Ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, Peyote, San Pedro, etc.). Study procedures will include a compilation of assessments online, as well as participation in online auditory, visual, and decision-making games.
  • Some assessments will ask about sensitive material pertaining to mental health including symptoms of anxiety, depression, psychosis, and substance use disorder.
  • No visits into our office are required as participation will be entirely web-based.
  • Your participation will take approximately 1 hour. Breaks can be taken at your discretion as you need them.
  • The only risks for participating in this study are potential boredom or tiredness after taking the entire assessment without breaks or potential discomfort in answering some of the questions, as some of them do have to do with your beliefs, your history, and your mental health.
  • There are no expected personal benefits for participation. In terms of benefits to society, we hope that this study will increase our understanding of the therapeutic effects and potential risks of psychedelics while potentially contributing to our overall understanding of the mechanisms of hallucinations in the brain. We hope that this will help us develop improved treatments for a variety of mental health conditions.
  •  Taking part in this study is your choice. You can choose to take part, or you can choose not to take part in this study. You can also change your mind at any time. Whatever choice you make, you will not lose access to your medical care or give up any legal rights or benefits.
  • If you are interested in learning more about the study, please continue reading, or have someone read to you, the rest of this document. Take as much time as you need before you make your decision. Ask the study staff questions about anything you do not understand. Once you understand the study, we will ask you if you wish to participate; if so, you will have to sign this form.

 

Why is this study being offered to me?

We are asking you to take part in a research study because you have regular computer and internet access and may or may not regularly use cannabis or psychedelics. We are looking for 400 healthy participants in this study.

Your participation in this study is extremely valuable for our research, and we hope that participating will prove to be an educational experience for you.  In addition, however, please remember that this is only one of the ways in which you can fulfill your "experimental participation" credits for Introduction to Psychology.  Other ways, as detailed in the form handed out to you in class, include serving as an observer of 5 experiments, or arranging for other options of equivalent educational value (e.g., writing essays) through your instructor.

What is the study about?

The purpose of this study is to understand possible differences in perception and belief formation that may exist between people who do and do not use psychedelics or cannabis to understand the potential risks and benefits to mental health of these compounds.

What are you asking me to do and how long will it take?

If you agree to take part in this study, this is what will happen: You will read this consent form and if you choose to participate, you will sign the consent form. Upon completion of consent, you will then be sent a link to your email address where you will have access to the eligibility screening questionnaire for the study. Screening you for eligibility will allow us to determine which assessments may be most beneficial for you to take. Personal information may be gathered such as first name, email address, location, age, and sex, as well as mental health history.

After the screening, should you not be eligible for this part of the study, a screen will appear and you will be notified that at this time we cannot proceed. You will not be able to move forward with the surveys. Should you be eligible to participate, you will be presented with a series of other assessments based on how you answered the questions in the screening process, as well as the hearing and vision games. This entire process will take about 30-60 minutes (if you were to take it all in one sitting); all of which you will be paid for (unless you are Yale student, in which case you receive only course credit). Please note you are encouraged to take as many breaks as you need.

Once we have received all of your responses from the assessments and the games, we will carefully review them to ensure we understand your responses so that the data can be correctly interpreted for our research. Should we have any follow up questions, we will be reaching out to you for clarification. Additionally, we will be doing quality control of responses to the games and there is a chance you may need to re-play the games if we feel you may not have understood how to respond correctly or if there's any indication in your performance that you were unable to provide answers that made sense. 

What are the risks and discomforts of participating?

There are minimal to no risks in participation. The potential risks are boredom or tiredness from the length of time this can take, so we encourage you to take breaks as often, and as long as you need. Some of the questions may even be uncomfortable because they do ask personal information. Our research team is available to you at any time to discuss any discomfort you may be experiencing or to answer any questions you have.

 For Yale students, the following protocol is in place to offer support for students based on their answers to questions pertaining to mental health:

Several additional steps will be taken as part of a plan to handle incidental findings with respect to apparent depression, severe anxiety, problematic substance use, distressing hallucinations, or suicidality should they arise. First, the investigator receiving the submitted depression/anxiety/hallucination/delusion measures is a qualified, clinically trained post-clerkship MD/PhD student who is closely advised by his PI who is himself a board-certified psychiatrist and has close access to a child and adolescent psychiatry fellow. RedCap sends email notifications to this investigator with each completed survey, and responses are reviewed within 24 hours.  Participants will be identified and contacted in the event that their answers demonstrate: 1) elevated depression scores (5 or greater on PHQ9) and who endorse mild suicidality (greater than a 0 item 9 on the PHQ-9 ), 2) severe anxiety (BAI > 26), 3) endorsement of distress related to hallucinations on Chicago Hallucination Assessment Tool (CHAT) or Auditory Hallucinations Rating Scale (AHRS), or 4) endorsement that they may have a problematic relationship with a substance.

 

Dr. Albert Powers (a licensed psychiatrist) will follow-up on this information by personally contacting participants with any of the above criteria. PHQ-9 and BAI scores were chosen based on standardized scores for clinical severity of mood and anxiety symptoms. Endorsed distress and problematic relationship with substances were selected as criteria for hallucination and substance-use reporting in recognition of the fact that presence of hallucinations or frequent substance use are often not experienced as disordered. Dr. Powers will contact participants by email with the following scripts:

 For participants who endorse elevated depressive symptoms in their survey: " I am a faculty supervisor and psychiatrist involved in the psychology experiment you did recently. The person who ran your experiment noticed that you seemed to be feeling quite down and blue, according to one of the questionnaires you completed. I wanted to follow-up and offer to provide any other referral information you might want. Additionally, if you would like to speak with me over the phone or in person, I would be glad to do so. Please let me know. Thanks."

 For participants who endorse elevated anxiety symptoms in their survey: " I am a faculty supervisor and psychiatrist involved in the psychology experiment you did recently. The person who ran your experiment noticed that you seemed to be feeling pretty stressed and worried, according to one of the questionnaires you completed. I wanted to follow-up and offer to provide any other referral information you might want. Additionally, if you would like to speak with me over the phone or in person, I would be glad to do so. Please let me know. Thanks."

For participants who endorse distressing hallucinations in their survey: " I am a faculty supervisor and psychiatrist involved in the psychology experiment you did recently. The person who ran your experiment noticed that you seemed to be having some unusual experiences that you've been struggling with, according to one of the questionnaires you completed. I wanted to follow-up and offer to provide any other referral information you might want. Additionally, if you would like to speak with me over the phone or in person, I would be glad to do so. Please let me know. Thanks."

For participants who endorse problematic substance use in their survey: "I am a faculty supervisor and psychiatrist involved in the psychology experiment you did recently. The person who ran your experiment noticed that you seemed to have some concerns about substance use, according to one of the questionnaires you completed. I wanted to follow-up and offer to provide any other referral information you might want. Additionally, if you would like to speak with me over the phone or in person, I would be glad to do so. Please let me know. Thanks."

Participants who respond to this phone call and/or email will be encouraged to make an appointment with the Yale Center for Anxiety and Mood Disorders (YCAMD), Psychosis Prodrome Research Clinic (PRIME), or Yale Health. YCAMD is conveniently located next to Yale University's campus; PRIME is in the Connecticut Mental Health Center next to the medical campus. Assistance in making appointments will be provided if requested. Those requesting referrals outside the University will be given a list of referrals based on Dr. Powers's familiarity with local specialists in mood and anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, or psychotic-spectrum disorders.

How will I know about new risks or important information about the study?

We will tell you if we learn any new information that could change your mind about taking part in this study.

 How can the study possibly benefit me?

There are no expected personal benefits for participation. 

How can the study possibly benefit other people?

In terms of benefits to society, we hope that this study will increase our understanding of the therapeutic effects and potential risks of psychedelics while potentially contributing to our overall understanding of the mechanisms of hallucinations in the brain. We hope that this will help us develop improved treatments for a variety of mental health conditions.

Are there any costs to participation?

You will not have to pay for taking part in this study. The study will be taking place in the comfort of your own home or space of choice, so there will be no costs for transportation either.

 Will I be paid for participation?

Participants recruited as a Yale students will not receive compensation for this study.

What are my choices if I decide not to take part in this study?

Instead of participating in this study, you can choose not to.

How will you keep my data safe and private?

We will keep information we collect about you confidential. We will share it with others if you agree to it or when we have to do it because U.S. or State law requires it. For example, we will tell somebody if we learn that you are hurting a child or an older person. Information collected about substance use history will be kept confidential and will not be shared with law enforcement or anyone outside the research team.

 When we publish the results of the research or talk about it in conferences, we will not use your name. If we want to use your name, we would ask you for your permission. 

 We will not use your information or distribute it for future research studies without your permission.

 While we will be collecting your first name, email address and state of residence, all of your information will be de-identified upon receipt and only the study team will have access to your personal information. We will also be keeping this data for ten years before destroying it.

What Information Will You Collect About Me in this Study?

 The information we are asking to use and share is called "Protected Health Information." It is protected by a federal law called the Privacy Rule of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). In general, we cannot use or share your health information for research without your permission. If you want, we can give you more information about the Privacy Rule. Also, if you have any questions about the Privacy Rule and your rights, you can speak to Yale Privacy Officer at 203-432-5919.

 The specific information about you and your health that we will collect, use, and share includes: age, sex, race, medical history, diagnoses, substance use, and results of the study.

  •  Research study records
  • Records about your study visits
  • Information obtained during this research regarding
  • Questionnaires
  • The diagnosis and treatment of a mental health condition

 

How will you use and share my information?

We will use your information to conduct the study described in this consent form.

We may share your information with:

  • The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) agencies
  • Representatives from Yale University, the Yale Human Research Protection Program and the Institutional Review Board (the committee that reviews, approves, and monitors research on human participants), who are responsible for ensuring research compliance.  These individuals are required to keep all information confidential.
  • Co-Investigators and other investigators
  • Study Coordinator and Members of the Research Team
  • Data and Safety Monitoring Boards and others authorized to monitor the conduct of the Study

 We will do our best to make sure your information stays private. But, if we share information with people who do not have to follow the Privacy Rule, your information will no longer be protected by the Privacy Rule. Let us know if you have questions about this. However, to better protect your health information, agreements are in place with these individuals and/or companies that require that they keep your information confidential.

 

Why must I sign this document?

By signing this form, you will allow researchers to use and disclose your information described above for this research study. This is to ensure that the information related to this research is available to all parties who may need it for research purposes. You always have the right to review and copy your health information in your medical record.

 

What if I change my mind?

The authorization to use and disclose your health information collected during your participation in this study will never expire.  However, you may withdraw or take away your permission at any time. You may withdraw your permission by telling the study staff or by writing to Dr. Al Powers at the Yale University, New Haven, CT 06520.

 

If you withdraw your permission, you will not be able to stay in this study but the care you get from your doctor outside this study will not change.  No new health information identifying you will be gathered after the date you withdraw. Information that has already been collected may still be used and given to others until the end of the research study to insure the integrity of the study and/or study oversight. 

 

What if I want to refuse or end participation before the study is over?

 Taking part in this study is your choice. You can choose to take part, or you can choose not to take part in this study.  You also can change your mind at any time.  Whatever choice you make, you will not lose access to your medical care or give up any legal rights or benefits.

Not participating or withdrawing later will not harm your relationship with your own doctors or with this institution. 

 To withdraw from the study, you can call or email a member of the research team at any time and tell them that you no longer want to take part.  You can also simply stop participation by no longer filling out the online surveys or no longer logging in to participate in other surveys.

The researchers may withdraw you from participating in the research if necessary due to exclusion criteria.

 

What will happen with my data if I stop participating?

Should you stop participating, whatever data has been collected within the surveys will still potentially be used.

 

Who should I contact if I have questions?

Please feel free to ask about anything you don't understand. If you have questions later or if you have a research-related problem, you can call the Principal Investigator at  203- 974-7329.

You may also email the research team at powers.lab@yale.edu.

If you have questions about your rights as a research participant, or you have complaints about this research, you call the Yale Institutional Review Boards at (203) 785-4688 or email hrpp@yale.edu.

Yale students -- skip this section.

You are doing AMAZING! Thank you again for all of the hard work you are continuing to put into this study!

We want to understand how psychedelics might cause different positive and negative effects in different people. One variable that may be critical to consider is one's history of traumatic life experiences. We know that it is often painful to talk about trauma, and so we only require a single question just to know -- in the vaguest sense possible -- if you have every experienced any trauma at three points in your life.

If you feel comfortable sharing more information about your experiences, then you can optionally do so, and we will put the information towards research designed to help people experiencing mental illness, including trauma-induced illness.

Regardless, we want you to know that there many other resources out there for you if you feel like you need someone to talk to or peers to connect with. Here are some great resources that are all over the U.S. and other areas of the world:

U.S. and Canada:

https://www.traumasurvivorsnetwork.org/pages/our-centers

https://www.mhanational.org/find-support-groups

https://www.nami.org/Learn-More/Mental-Health-Conditions/Posttraumatic-Stress-Disorder/Support


International:

Participants who have used psychedelics have reported fascinating, non-distressing hallucination-like visual experiences after using psychedelics (eg. breathing objects, moving patterns, more visual intensity, etc.).
We want to know about other sensory experiences people may have after using psychedelics outside just what they see.
Have you ever noted NEW unusual experiences in your HEARING (sounds, noises, audition, etc.) that started AFTER a psychedelic experience, when you were NO LONGER high?
This does NOT count times when (1) you were under the influence of another psychoactive drug or (2) you were in a trance, falling asleep, waking up, or had not slept in a long time, or (3) you were experiencing known symptoms of a psychotic spectrum disorder (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, schizoaffective disorder, schizophreniform disorder, etc.)

Please list, in a numbered list, any changes you've had in your HEARING (sounds, noises, audition, etc.) in the days, weeks, or years after psychedelic use. Please provide as much detail surroudning the experience as you are willing to offer with regard to what the experience was, what triggered it, how long it lasted, how frequent it was, and how long you've had experiences like it since psychedelic use. You may also include additional details that you think may be worth noting. Please just include each on its own numbered line. 
    For example: 
    1. Processed foods tasted worse. This started after LSD when I was 22 and is present now. It is constant. 
    2. I randomly tasted metal three times after one DMT experience at 45. The last time this happened was 4 days after the DMT. It came out of the blue and lasted for 1-5 seconds...
    3. Etc.

Section Header:
Difficult Life Experiences

You are doing AMAZING! Thank you again for all of the hard work you are continuing to put into this study!

We want to understand how psychedelics might cause different positive and negative effects in different people. One variable that may be critical to consider is one's history of traumatic life experiences. We know that it is often painful to talk about trauma, and so we only require a single question just to know -- in the vaguest sense possible -- if you have every experienced any trauma at three points in your life.

If you feel comfortable sharing more information about your experiences, then you can optionally do so, and we will put the information towards research designed to help people experiencing mental illness, including trauma-induced illness.

Regardless, we want you to know that there many other resources out there for you if you feel like you need someone to talk to or peers to connect with. Here are some great resources that are all over the U.S. and other areas of the world:

U.S. and Canada:

https://www.traumasurvivorsnetwork.org/pages/our-centers

https://www.mhanational.org/find-support-groups

https://www.nami.org/Learn-More/Mental-Health-Conditions/Posttraumatic-Stress-Disorder/Support


International:

https://www.colleaga.org/article/list-ptsd-organizations-and-resources

A traumatic experience is an event, series of events, or set of circumstances that is experienced by an individual as physically or emotionally harmful or life threatening and that has lasting adverse effects on the individual's functioning and mental, physical, social, emotional, or spiritual well-being.
-Examples of traumatic experiences include, but are not limited to: 
-Experiencing or observing physical, sexual, and emotional abuse
-Childhood neglect
-Having a family member with a mental health or substance use disorder
-Experiencing or witnessing violence in the community or while serving in the military
-Poverty and systemic discrimination.
